div.p: The paper presents a decoupled scheduling approach for distributed hard real-time embedded automotive systems while considering schedulability and extensibility. Here the extensibility is defined as the adaptivity of the schedules to changes resulting from later upgrades. The idea is to use the time-slicing technique to assign transmission timewindows for messages on the bus so that the precedence relations between different processors are enforced by those time-window assignments, and the scheduling problems for each processor and the bus are decoupled. Thus, the existing uni-processor scheduling methods can be applied. The most innovative aspect of the approach in this paper is that the system level consideration is provided in determining those time-windows for the extensibility of the schedules and the schedulability on each individual processor.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The design process of embedded automotive systems typically involves the following two stages: control logic/algorithm design that is performed by control engineers, and software implementation that is performed by software engineers. Typical activities of software engineers include decomposing the necessary computational activities into tasks, assigning tasks to ECUs (Electrical Control Units), scheduling the tasks on each ECU and the messages on the communication buses to meet the desired hard real-time constraints under the given hardware performance, and achieving the desired degree of fault tolerance through replication and error correction. In the software implementation stage, the task and message scheduling problem is very important.

For the automotive embedded system scheduling, we believe that the complexity (time and memory needed) for scheduling and the extensibility (adaptivity to changes) of the obtained schedules are very important, since the reusability is a main focus in the automotive system design for various reasons, and a schedule with good extensibility means that we can reuse the previous design with only some minor modifications. Complexity is important because for distributed systems generally it is intractable to search the complete solution space, thus we need an approach with good complexity. For distributed scheduling, there are several different approaches such as heuristic scheduling ( [4], [5], [7]), holistic priority based scheduling ( [10], [3]), branch and bound search based scheduling ( [2], [6], [11]), offsetbased approach ( [9]), and slicing-based scheduling ( [8]). However, no existing approach considers the extensibility requirement in scheduling explicitly. In this paper, we try to provide an approach for scheduling of distributed hard realtime embedded systems while considering the schedulability and extensibility.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section II, the distributed scheduling problem is described, and a decoupled distributed scheduling approach is presented with the consideration of schedulability and extensibility. In Section III, an illustrative example is supplied. Section IV concludes the paper.

div.head: II. DECOUPLED DISTRIBUTED SCHEDULING
div.p: We first describe the problem and then present the solution.

div.head: A. Problem description
div.p: We consider the extensible scheduling for distributed hard real-time embedded systems. The system consists of a number of processors that are connected through a communication bus. There is also a set of software tasks that are allocated to the different processors, and tasks on different nodes may communicate with each other via messages transmitted on the communication bus. These software tasks are periodic tasks and have hard deadlines. Failure to meet a hard deadline is catastrophic. There are also precedence constraints among the tasks, e.g., one task may need to be executed before the execution of another task within one execution cycle/period because of the precedence relation between them. We need to schedule the task executions on each processor and the message transmissions on the bus so that all the deadlines are met and all the constraints, like precedence constraints, are satisfied. We also want the schedules derived to be extensible, i.e., if some changes are needed after the implementation of the system, such as adding/removing processors/tasks for the purpose of upgrade, the remaining schedules would better not be affected. For example, if the task set is changed at one processor or a new processor is added to the system, then we do not want this change to impact the schedules on other processors. If we find out that this change will not affect the bus schedule of all existing messages, i.e., the new messages can be transmitted on the bus without affecting the transmissions of existing messages, then no change is needed for schedules at other processors. Otherwise, we may need to rebuild the bus schedule and thus may need to rebuild the schedules for the whole system; and this is what we try to avoid.

The above distributed scheduling problem can be described more precisely as follows. There are m processors and N tasks. These tasks are already allocated to the m processors. The task set is denoted by
div.formula: {t ij , i = 1, • • • , m, j = 1, • • • , n i }, where tasks {t ij , j = 1, • • • , n i }
div.p: are allocated to the processor p i , and m i=1 n i = N . For each task t ij , let A ij be its arrival time, C ij be its worst case execution time, D ij be its deadline, and T ij be its period with T ij ≥ D ij . There are precedence relations among the tasks. These relations are represented as "t ij precedes t kl " (also denoted by t ij → t kl ), which means that the task t ij must be executed before the task t kl within one period (assuming they have the same period). We need to schedule the task executions on each processor so that all the deadlines are met, all the precedence constraints are satisfied, and the schedules derived shall be extensible to later upgrades.
Without loss of generality, we make the following two assumptions.

1) There is no communication delay between the tasks, i.e., the output of a task t ij can be transmitted to another task t kl as input without delay. 2) All tasks have the same period, i.e., T ij = T for all i and j. The first assumption comes from the fact that we can model the communication bus as a special processor, and messages transmitted on the bus can be viewed as tasks to be executed on this bus processor. For example, if task t ij needs to send a message m ij-kl to task t kl over the bus because of the precedence relation "t ij → t kl ", then we can view the bus as a processor p c and the message m ij-kl as a task to be executed on p c . Then, the precedence relation "t ij → t kl " is replaced by "t ij → m ij-kl → t kl ". Accordingly, we can let the execution time of m ij-kl equal its transmission time, let the period of m ij-kl be the same as the period of t ij and t kl (assuming they have the same period), let the arrival time of m ij-kl be the same as the arrival time of t ij , and let the deadline of m ij-kl be the same as the deadline of t kl . Note that the actual arrival time of m ij-kl shall be the finishing time of t ij and the actual deadline of m ij-kl shall be the starting time of t kl . However, under the precedence constraint "t ij → m ij-kl → t kl ", letting the arrival time of m ij-kl be the same as the arrival time of t ij and letting the deadline of m ij-kl be the same as the deadline of t kl have the same effects as letting the arrival time of m ij-kl be the finishing time of t ij and letting the deadline of m ij-kl be the starting time of t kl , so it is okay for us to make the above choices for the arrival time and deadline of m ij-kl .

The second assumption comes from the fact that the scheduling problem for tasks with different periods can always be transformed to one for tasks with a common period. If the tasks have different periods, since we only need to solve the scheduling problem for the time interval that is equal to the least common multiple of the periods of all tasks, we can treat every invocation of each task within the interval as a new task, and all these new tasks have the same period that is equal to the least common multiple of the periods of all old tasks. Then instead of solving the scheduling problem for the set of old tasks with different periods, we can solve the scheduling problem for the set of new tasks with a common period.

As we mentioned above, one difficulty in distributed scheduling is the complexity. The complexity of the distributed scheduling mainly comes from the coupling of each individual processor scheduling. This coupling results from the precedence relations among tasks on different processors. Thus, one way to solve the distributed scheduling is to decouple each individual processor scheduling by enforcing the precedence relations through time-slicing, i.e., assigning explicit time-windows for the transmission of messages on the bus. Once the transmission time-windows are determined for the messages, then we can use the existing results on uni-processor scheduling for each individual processor scheduling, i.e., the distributed scheduling is decoupled to a set of uni-processor scheduling problems that can be solved by existing uni-processor scheduling techniques.

The decoupling approach works as follows: for each message m ij-kl on the bus assign a time-window [b ij-kl , e ij-kl ] for its transmission such that all the precedence constraints among different processors are satisfied by the assignments and all the necessary timing requirements are satisfied.

In the following, we first describe the constraints that the message time-windows must satisfy, and then we define an objective function that captures the schedulability and the extensibility so that the determination of the message time-windows becomes an optimization problem with linear constraints and non-linear objective function.

The procedure given in the above algorithm for G ij is correct by considering the fact that those tasks are executed on the same processor. It is easy to find out that by following the procedure, we have G ij = 0 for the above example, which is correct. A similar procedure is also provided for F ij in the above algorithm.

div.head: C. Objective function for schedulability and extensibility
div.p: The question remains is how to determine b ij-kl and e ij-kl for the schedulability and the extensibility, i.e., how to determine b ij-kl and e ij-kl so that it is more feasible to schedule tasks on each individual processor and the schedules derived are more extensible to changes for later upgrades. In other words, the time-window determination problem is a constrained optimization problem, where the constraints are represented by four equations given above, and the objectives for optimization are schedulability and extensibility. We need to define an objective function for schedulability and extensibility. We find out that the schedulability and the extensibility is related to the peak and average processor usage requests of tasks. The objective function is derived based on the peak and average processor usage requests of tasks in the following.
First, let us define the processor usage request function for each task
div.formula: t ij , f ij (t) : [0, T ] → R, f ij (t) = Cij weij -wbij t ∈ [wb ij , we ij ] 0 otherwise
div.p: where T is the common period, R is the set of real numbers, C ij is the worst case execution time of t ij , [wb ij , we ij ] is the processor usage window requested by t ij that is determined from the message transmission windows by the following algorithm.

Algorithm 2: Algorithm for obtaining wb ij and we ij 1) For message tasks m ij-kl on the bus, wb ij-kl = b ij-kl and we ij-kl = e ij-kl . 2) For tasks t ij on each non-bus processor p i , starting from the tasks having no successor on processor p i and processing on every step those tasks whose successors on p i have been processed:
div.formula: we ij = ⎧ ⎪ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎪ ⎩ min{E ij , min l:tij →til we il }, ∃(q, r) s.t. t ij → m ij-qr min{E ij , min (q,r) wb ij-qr , Y }, otherwise Y = min (u,v):tij →tir 1 →•••tir k →mir k -uv (wb irk-uv - k h=1 C irh ).
div.p: 3) For tasks t ij on each non-bus processor p i , starting from the tasks having no predecessor on processor p i and processing on every step those tasks whose predecessors on p i have been processed:
div.formula: wb ij = ⎧ ⎪ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎪ ⎩ max{B ij , max l:til→tij wb il }, ∃(q, r) s.t. m qr-ij → t ij max{B ij , max (q,r) we qr-ij , Z}, otherwise Z = max (u,v):muv-ir 1 →tir 1 •••→tir k →tij (we uv-ir1 + k h=1 C ih ).
div.p: In the above computation of we ij , when the task t ij does not have any immediate successor on other processors, i.e., there does not exist (q, r) such that t ij → m ij-qr , one can also use we ij = min{E ij , min l:tij →til (we il -C il )} instead of what is used in the algorithm. The intent of our above decision in the algorithm is that when the task t ij does not have any immediate successor on other processors, we want to combine the tasks t ij and its successors on the same processor, i.e., the task t il , as one super task for the computation of the usage request function, which is a fact followed directly from our choice by trying to assign the same usage window for the two tasks. Since our main purpose is to identify the time-windows for the messages on the bus so that the scheduling on each processor can be decoupled, we are not trying to schedule each individual task at this moment. The task scheduling on each individual processor is performed after the time-windows for the messages are determined. Here, the determination of the processor usage window for each task will lead to the computation of the usage request function, which will be used for the determination of the time-windows for the messages on the bus later. Because the task t ij has no immediate successor on other processors, implying that it has no direct impact on the time-windows of the messages on the bus, it follows naturally that we want to combine t ij with its successors for the computation of the usage request function by trying to assign the same usage window for t ij and its successors, which would eventually help to simplify the determination of the time-windows for the messages on the bus. The same line of thinking applies to our decision in the above algorithm for the computation of wb ij when the task t ij does not have any immediate predecessor on other processors.
Next, let us define the usage request function for each processor p i ,
div.formula: g i (t) : [0, T ] → R, g i (t) = ni j=1 f ij (t)
div.p: Then the peak usage request for each processor is defined as
div.formula: P U i = max t∈[0,T ] g i (t),
div.p: and it is not difficult to find out that
div.formula: P U i = max t∈{wbij ,j=1,•••,ni} g i (t)
div.p: The average usage request for each processor is defined as
div.formula: AU i = T 0 g 2 i (t)dt T 0 g i (t)dt Since T 0 f ij (t)dt = C ij , we have AU i = T 0 g 2 i (t)dt
O(b ij-kl , e ij-kl ) = m i=1 α i (P U 2 i + AU 2 i )
div.p: where m i=1 α i = 1, α i is the weight for processor p i , and they are determined by the system designer. In general, we can let α i = 1/m. If the schedulability and the extensibility of a processor (like the processor for the bus) is more important, then the corresponding weight for the processor can be increased.

The reason we use the usage requests as the objective function is that the value of resource (processor and bus) usage request represents the level of the contention for the resources. If we can balance the usage requests among all the resources (processors/bus) and over the whole execution period (by minimizing the average and peak usage request), then we can reduce the contention for the resources on each processor/bus and at each moment over the whole execution period, which will make each individual processor/bus scheduling much easier. Because the contention for the resources is reduced, it would be easier to add tasks/processors within the existing schedule without changing it. Thus, the above objective function captures the schedulability as well as extensibility.

div.p: Remark 1: Note that when the above decoupled scheduling approach is applied to a given system, there may not exist feasible schedule for certain individual processor based on the derived message time-windows, which only means that the system is not schedulable by the decoupled scheduling approach. In other words, when the decoupled scheduling approach fails to schedule a given system, the system could still be schedulable by other approaches. So the above decoupled scheduling approach can be viewed as a heuristic approach. Because of the following reasons, the above is a good scheduling approach for the automotive embedded systems.

• The development of automotive embedded systems usually involves multiple suppliers, which requires that some resource sharing decisions (such as the bus bandwidth or the bus message slot assignments) must be made before the system integration so that each supplier can go ahead and develop their own sub-systems. The decoupled scheduling approach aligns very well with the above development process involving multiple suppliers.

• Because of the nature of the earlier decision making in the above development process, there is a lot of uncertainties for the values of system parameters such as the worst case execution time of tasks, so it requires that the schedules derived shall be robust. Also because of the reusability requirement in the automotive embedded systems, the schedules shall be extensible. In the decoupled scheduling, the schedules for all the individual processors are decoupled from each other based on the message time-windows. So as long as the message timewindows derived are robust and extensible, the system schedule is robust and extensible. Since it is much easier to change a decoupled individual processor schedule than to change multiple coupled processor schedules.

In the above, the message time-windows are derived by considering the robustness and extensibility, which is clear from the definition of the objective function. • The automotive embedded systems usually involve many processors. So the complexity is important in scheduling. It is not difficult to find out that the above decoupled scheduling approach has a linear complexity in the number of processors.

div.head: D. The issue of synchronization
div.p: In the above, we adopt a time-slicing approach to decouple the multi-processor scheduling. However, the above time-slicing approach does not necessarily require a synchronized clock for all processors. In other words, our results could be applied to both time-triggered systems like FlexRay and event-triggered systems like CAN. For time-triggered systems like systems with FlexRay buses that have a globally synchronized clock, the above time-slicing approach can be applied directly, i.e., those time-windows are honored according to the global clock. For systems without a globally synchronized clock such as systems with CAN buses, we can use messages for synchronization. This is explained in more detail below.

Suppose we have two tasks t i1 and t k1 on two different processors (p i and p k ) that communicate via the message m i1-k1 on the CAN bus, i.e., we have the precedence constraints of "t i1 precedes m i1-k1 " and "m i1-k1 precedes t k1 ". After applying the approach in this paper, suppose we have the following time-windows for t i1 , m i1-k1 , and t • On processor p i , let T end i1 be the actual finishing time of t i1 according to the clock of p i , then the message m i1-kl will not be released for transmission on the CAN bus until the time max {T end i1 , b i1-k1 } according to the clock of p i .

• On processor p k , let T receive k1 be the actual receiving time of message m i1-k1 according to the clock of p k , then the task t k1 will not be released for execution until the time max {T receive k1 , b k1 } according to the clock of p k . For the above message synchronization approach to work correctly, we have the following requirements.
• The clocks of all processors are synchronized initially.

• In the uni-processor scheduling for the given timewindows like [b ij , e ij ], there shall be a release jitter Δt for each task whose releasing depends on a message from the CAN bus and for each message on the CAN bus, such that the task/message is released within the window
div.formula: [b ij , b ij + Δt].
div.p: This release jitter is used to capture the effect of the later arrival of messages because of the time drift of the un-synchronized clocks. In general, we can let Δt be the maximal time drift of the un-synchronized clocks within the system continuous operation period. (Note that for automotive applications the system continuous operation time is usually a number of hours because of the refill for gasoline. So the maximal time drift within a number of hours will not be a very big number.) The above two conditions are not difficult to satisfy in implementations and the uni-processor scheduling approaches for tasks with release jitters are well developed. It is also not difficult to find out that the precedence relations are enforced by the above message synchronization approach.

div.head: III. AN ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE
div.p: In this section, we provide an example to illustrate the approaches developed in this paper. The example is modified from a control application that has been used several times in the literature of distributed scheduling [8], [1], [6].

The system consists of a sensory device mounted on a motorized platform that must detect and track specific objects in the environment. The system is controlled by four processors connected by a single bus. The application software consists of six processes broken into 22 tasks plus six messages on the bus. The six processes are the Main Control Process on processor p 1 , the Sensor Manager Process and the Sensor Process on processor p 2 that are responsible for the control of the sensor, the Actuator Manager Process and the Actuator Control Process on processor p 3 that are responsible for the control of the actuators, and the Signal Process on processor p 4 that is responsible for the management of the significant events that are detected in the environment (e.g., alarm generation). The control flow of the application is given as Figure 1, where each node in the figure is labeled with the corresponding task identifier t ij and the worst case execution time C ij (value in the circle). The common period is 100. All tasks have an arrival time A ij = 0, and all tasks have a deadline of 100 (same as the period) except that the deadline of t 27 is 40 (i.e., D 27 = 40). We need to schedule the tasks on each processor and the messages on the bus such that all the precedence constraints and the deadlines are satisfied. To solve the above scheduling problem using the approach developed in this paper, we need first to determine the time-window for each message on the bus, then perform the task/message scheduling for each processor/bus independently. First, let us use Algorithm 1 to obtain the earliest starting time and the latest ending time for each task and message. We have the results as shown in Table I, where EST stands for earliest starting time and LET stands for latest ending time.
Next, we use Algorithm 2 to obtain the requested usage window for each task from the message transmission windows, which is shown in Table II.

Then we can obtain the processor usage request function f ij (t) for each task/message, the usage request function g i (t) for each processor/bus, the peak and average usage requests P U i and AU i for each processor/bus, and finally the objective function
div.formula: O(b ij-kl , e ij-kl ) = 5 i=1 0.2 * (P U 2 i + AU 2 i ).
div.p: Next we need to solve the optimization problem for the determination of the time-window [b ij-kl , e ij-kl ] for each message m ij-kl . After solving the above optimization problem, we obtain the time-windows for the messages on the bus as shown in Table III. Now the original scheduling problem is decoupled into five individual uni-processor/bus scheduling problems and can be solved by using many existing techniques. The details are omitted here. The fact that each decoupled individual processor is schedulable for the derived time-windows of messages indicates that the schedulability is well considered by our decoupled scheduling approach.

In order to show that our solution is extensible to the addition of tasks, let us assume that one more task is added in the Main Control process on processor p 1 between the tasks t 12 and t 13 with a worst case execution time of 10. It is easy to check that we can still schedule the newly added task on p 1 without changing the time-windows for all the bus messages, which implies that we need not change the bus schedule and the task schedules on all other processors. To see this more clearly, the old and new task schedules for processor p 1 are provided in Table IV.

To show that the schedulability of each individual processor is well considered in our decoupled approach for different scenarios, let us assume that there is another task t 44 is added on processor p 4 with A 44 = 80, C 44 = 15, and D 44 = 100 (note that now there is no task between t 12 and t 13 ). From our approach the new time-windows for the bus messages can be obtained as shown in Table V, and it is not difficult to check that the five decoupled processors/bus are still schedulable. IV. CONCLUSION

In the distributed scheduling of hard real-time systems like the automotive embedded systems, complexity and extensibility are two very important issues. This paper presents a new time-slicing based decoupling approach for the distributed scheduling of hard real-time embedded systems. System level consideration is provided in determining the time-windows of bus messages for the schedulability and the extensibility. As a result, the schedulability of each decoupled processor is well considered and the schedules derived are extensible to changes from later upgrades.
